name: Uma Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the line crew that covers the ridge roads and the small estates below them. My two-year technical diploma is useful when a fault hops between feeders, but experience tells me when the drawing is lying. I allocate the climb, check the isolation, and still go up myself when a repair is awkward. My partner Ren gets our two children to school when I am called out early; with the mortgage and less than a month of expenses saved, even a steady week can feel too long before payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a quicker form is welcome, but nobody signs an isolation sheet without checking the equipment. A computer can shorten my notes; it cannot hear a loose connection crackle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our pay is low for a lead, and we have almost no reserve beyond this month. Even a small mistake that cancels a callout would hurt us, though the plateau itself does not threaten the linework.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the usual repair rota and compare any generated work orders with my field notebook. After each payday I would put a small fixed amount into a separate emergency account if the mortgage and food are covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am uneasy already, without needing a robot to explain it. The bank balance is what I picture when the truck will not start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much could you set aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start with twenty from each payday if the bills allow it. A larger promise would be fiction in our kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for different software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not yet. I use an AI tool occasionally to shorten a notice, but I would first see whether the company form makes fewer mistakes than my own notes.

say: **Faster forms** are useful only when the crew still verifies isolation.
**Field sounds** and measurements remain part of fault finding.
think: Our **thin reserve** makes any missed callout matter.
The **plateau** leaves physical line repair broadly as it is.
do: **Keep** the repair rota and compare generated orders with the field notebook.
**Save** twenty from each payday if food and mortgage bills are covered.
feel: **Uneasy** about household money even with little AI change.
S0.quote: A computer can shorten my notes; it cannot hear a loose connection crackle.
fieldNote: Her **lead role** has not translated into a comfortable buffer or high pay.
She makes a **conditional saving** pledge tied to basic bills, not a claim about money already saved.

steps.text: Keep line repair rota and compare work orders with field notebook
Save twenty each payday if mortgage and food are covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the call desk and ordering team will change first, while my crew still tests and repairs lines. I want the union involved before software sets repair times from a clean map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A tighter schedule could strip our callout pay even if no lineworker is laid off. There are few similar jobs nearby, so I cannot simply take my diploma down the road and get the same hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep a month of actual repair times beside the proposed software times. In the first year I would bring the records to our union branch and ask them to press for a crew review of targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because losing callouts would hit the mortgage quickly. I can argue about a target, but I cannot manufacture another local employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the records show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would separate travel, isolation, repair and testing time for each job. The office might see only the drive and the repair on a map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change at home if callouts fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ren and I would cancel the weekend swimming trip before taking the children out of lessons. The small amount we have saved would not carry repeated short pays.

say: **Desk changes** arrive before automation of physical line repairs.
**Union review** should check software repair targets against real jobs.
think: Lost **callout pay** could threaten the mortgage before my base job disappears.
There are **few local jobs** to replace these hours.
do: **Log** travel, isolation, repair and testing times for a month.
**Bring** the log to the union branch to challenge shortened targets.
**Cancel** weekend trips if callout pay actually drops.
feel: **Anxious** about fewer paid hours and limited local alternatives.
S1.quote: I can argue about a target, but I cannot manufacture another local employer.
fieldNote: She separates **office automation** from the slower change to hands-on repair.
Her **union plan** uses measured job times, and her spending cut depends on lost callouts.

steps.text: Bring month of repair times to union branch for target review
Cancel weekend trips if callout pay drops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crews that thinking AI in 2028 might take the fault plans, but capable hands-on robots arrive about 2031. We would still be the ones on the poles in the gap, and that time should be used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At forty-three with a mortgage and less than a month saved, the gap looks like a countdown. My lead title will not pay the bills if a robot takes most climb and repair work in 2031, and nearby utilities are scarce.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union branch to seek paid training in network safety testing this winter. If the employer offers paid places with a real testing post, I would take one; after 2028 I would cut extras and apply for that post before the field machines arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed enough to lose sleep, though I would still run tomorrow’s crew safely. I cannot let the children see me rush a live line because I am worrying about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which extras would go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ren and I would stop restaurant meals and new clothes for ourselves in the first year after 2028. The children’s school needs and mortgage come first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no paid place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union to press for one and keep working the line crew. I cannot buy an expensive course on the chance of a vacancy.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes fault planning before field robots arrive around 2031.
**Paid training** must be offered while line crews still have work.
think: My **lead title** will not protect our income if robots take repair work.
A **thin buffer** and few nearby jobs leave little room to wait.
do: **Seek** a paid network safety testing place with a real opening.
**Cut** adult meals and clothes after 2028 while applying for testing if qualified.
feel: **Alarmed** about the mortgage, yet determined to keep crew safety first.
S2.quote: My lead title will not pay the bills if a robot takes most climb and repair work in 2031, and nearby utilities are scarce.
fieldNote: Her **training choice** depends on funded time and a real testing vacancy.
She expects **field exposure** later than the office change, but her low savings make the gap frightening.

steps.text: Ask union branch to seek paid network testing places
Take paid network testing course if tied to a real vacancy
Stop restaurant meals and new adult clothes purchases after 2028
Apply for network testing post after 2028 if qualified

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets us ask what jobs the company really expects to keep. The thinking system arrives in 2031, while robots able to do field work follow around 2034; I would not call those the same date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could become the person who signs off safe isolation if the utility still wants a human checker. But a new title means nothing unless the pay covers our mortgage and the post is here, where the children are settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask the branch to negotiate paid assessor training and a written pay scale. If a local assessor opening is confirmed, I would complete the course before 2031; in the first year after 2031 I would apply, otherwise stay on the crew while field work remains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but I can breathe with five years rather than two. I would rather have a written offer than a cheerful slide about future jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask to see in writing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The number of local assessor posts, paid training days and the wage. I would also ask who can refuse to clear an unsafe line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you move to a distant utility instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ren’s work and the children’s schools are here. We would discuss moving only if there were an actual offer that covered the mortgage and the costs of starting elsewhere.

say: **2031 thinking AI** and field robots around 2034 leave distinct preparation windows.
**Written posts** and wages matter more than promises about future work.
think: A **human safety checker** role may suit my lead skills if the utility keeps one.
The **mortgage and children** make a distant speculative move difficult.
do: **Negotiate** paid assessor training and a written local pay scale through the branch.
**Complete** training only for a confirmed local opening before 2031.
**Apply** for the assessor role after 2031 if trained and pay covers the mortgage.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to plan around a documented offer.
S3.quote: I would rather have a written offer than a cheerful slide about future jobs.
fieldNote: Her **five-year plan** is conditional on a local vacancy and mortgage-covering pay.
Her **union request** includes who can refuse unsafe clearance, not just wage protection.

steps.text: Ask union branch to negotiate paid assessor training and pay scale
Complete paid assessor course before 2031 if local opening is confirmed
Apply for local assessor role after 2031 if pay covers mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade would give crews time to train apprentices and shape the rules before thinking AI arrives in 2036. Field robots around 2039 should be tested with workers in the room, not just sold to the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be fifty-three in 2036, and I cannot assume our mortgage is gone or that we can retire. I might have the skills to supervise tests of the machines, but I would still need enough pay to carry our household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on the line crew now and ask for an annual mortgage review with Ren. During the first year after 2036 I would apply for a local robot safety assessor job only if training is paid, the job exists and its pay covers our bills; I would help the union write field test rules meanwhile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wary rather than terrified. A decade is long enough to ask whether the machines can handle a wet roadside repair, not just a tidy demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want in a field test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A crew should test the robot on a damaged line after rain, with a human able to stop it. I would want the failed attempts recorded as clearly as the successful ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you plan to retire early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. With our savings this thin, calling retirement early would be pretending the mortgage pays itself.

say: **Worker-led tests** should precede field robot use around 2039.
**Apprentices** still need physical line skills through the long runway.
think: At **fifty-three**, I may still need strong pay and an unfinished mortgage.
A **safety assessor** post is possible only if the utility funds it.
do: **Review** the mortgage with Ren each year while staying on the crew.
**Apply** for local assessor work after 2036 only with paid training, a vacancy and bill-covering pay.
**Help** the union write robot field test rules.
feel: **Wary**, with time to demand credible field tests.
S4.quote: With our savings this thin, calling retirement early would be pretending the mortgage pays itself.
fieldNote: She explicitly rejects **early retirement** given the thin savings and continuing mortgage.
Her **assessor move** remains conditional on funded training, a real local job and sufficient pay.

steps.text: Keep line crew work and review mortgage with Ren annually
Apply for local assessor after 2036 only with paid training, vacancy and bill-covering pay
Help union write robot field test rules

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 scares me most, because we have almost no savings and only a few years between new fault systems and field robots. Paid training tied to a local job, plus a wage we can live on, would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You should ask who records the failures when a robot is tested. A glossy success count will not keep my crew safe.

portrait: **Uma Kowalski**, 43, leads an electricity line crew and has a two-year technical diploma.
She is among the **best lineworkers**, yet lower pay and less than a month saved leave her family exposed.
Partner Ren, two **school-age children** and a mortgage shape every decision about pay, time and local work.
She uses **AI occasionally**, trusts verified results and presses the union for realistic repair times and paid training.
The **2028 scenario** alarms her most; longer runways let her seek a local assessor role under firm conditions.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves too little time to build savings before capable field robots may cut repair work.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** linked to a genuine local assessor job would offer a path from field repairs.
A **bill-covering wage** and worker-led robot tests would protect her household and crew.
headlineQuote: A glossy success count will not keep my crew safe.
